text.p: Following are the main stories in Slovenia's Tuesday morning newspapers:
- The management of Slovenia's state-owned railways said a ten-day strike of railway employees, which started a week ago, has already cost the company some 300 million tolars ($2.0 million).

- Eleven members of the U.S. Congress visited Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek and the parliament on Monday to discuss Slovenia's bid to join NATO in the first round of the alliance's expansion.

- The Slovenian National Right Party has launched legal action against national television RTVS, claiming the party failed in last November's general election because of insufficient coverage. The party demands 25 million tolars in damages.
- Unions and employers said they may complete negotiations on a new general collective agreement, which determines work benefits, by Thursday. The previous agreement expires at the end of May.

- Employees at car maker Revoz, the Slovenian unit of France's Renault, held a one-hour strike on Monday, claiming work conditions had worsened since February when Renault announced it would close down its Belgian plant because of falling sales.
- Hans Dietrich Genscher, former German foreign minister, said Slovenia was one of the strongest candidates for NATO membership. Genscher visited Slovenia on Monday.
- Ljubljana mayor Dimitrij Rupel continues to push for the removal of Janez Sodrznik, director of the Ljubljana city council management, claiming his work is inefficient.
- Due to different accounting procedures daily allowances for state officials are almost twice as high as those paid to employees in private industry.
